speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Blue zones are the identified geographic communities where the inhabitants are known to have live well, live healthily, with exceptional life expectancies way higher than the world's average or higher than 80 years old.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I did some research on the article and noted that they also look at indicators, such as whether the people living in that communities live purposeful-driven life, the level of social connectivity, the low rates of chronic disease, healthy environment, among others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The BBC report also mentioned that Singapore's healthcare system has received global accolades both its quality of care and its ability to keep costs affordable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It also added that when it comes to longevity, Singapore is one of the few places in the world that saw quantum jump in life expectancies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The other five Blue Zone locations are Loma Linda in California, Nicoya Peninsula in Costa Rica, Sardina in Italy, Ikaria in Greece and Okinawa in Japan.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Interestingly, these locations are not known to be as fast-paced, vibrant cities like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They are more rural and country in nature with smaller populations and the tempo of life tend to be more relax.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, for Singapore to be named as a Blue Zone is really remarkable and we must have gotten the fundamentals and the policies right to achieve these excellent public outcomes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It must have provided Singaporeans a lot of convenience to be able to have access to so many countries and not to mention, the sense of pride to carry our red passport.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Again, we must have managed our foreign relations well to earn all these visa-free accesses and also that these countries do see Singaporeans as valued and desired tourists or visitors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thirdly, I would like to mention that the Singapore Public Service has recently also come out on top, in terms of performances among the 120 public administrations around the world; which included many developed countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have these international accolades, but it is good to also hear the inside view of how we see the Public Service has fared and the public sector outcomes as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As we transition to a greener and more sustainable future, can I ask the Minister a few questions in relation to how the MOF agencies are addressing issues of climate change and environmental sustainability?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What are public financing levers to steer Singapore towards our net-zero commitment?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Does the Government take environmental sustainability considerations into account when procuring goods and services, and can the Government do more?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Businesses are still trying to make the green transition and may not be able to meet the various environmental sustainability requirements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask what support is the Government providing to help these businesses?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Has the Public Sector adopted green budgeting and consider environmental sustainability in the management of public finances?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The headlines last month rang loud and clear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That will see close to six consecutive years of resale prices going up and further up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: HDB resale prices jumped 12.7% in 2021, 10.4% in 2022, 4.9% in 2023 and 9.7% in 2024.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In April last year, the Minister for National Development said that the Government expected the property market to continue stabilising.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He noted that resale HDB prices had risen less in 2023 at 4.9%, compared to 10.4% and 12.7% in the previous two years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At that time, which was a mere 11-odd months ago, the Minister attributed the slower price rise, which I should point out is still a significant price rise, to HDB having caught up on construction delays and a ramping up of Build-To-Order (BTO) flat launches.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was despite cooling measures being introduced in August last year, such as lowering the loan to valuation limit for HDB housing loans from 80% to 75%.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On another front, 2024 was an unusual year for Government Land Sales (GLS) sites for non-HDB use.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Last year, the Government rejected three tenders for three private residential sites because it deemed the sold bids for them to be too low.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Partly because of this, land betterment rates for non-landed residential use sites dropped by an average of 5.4% for the half-year from September 2024 to February 2025.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Chief Valuer (CV) reviews the Land Betterment Charge (LBC) rates twice a year in March and September, and the rates can be a barometer of the Government's assessment of land values in recent land sales.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The CV's work on land not sold for HDB purposes is highly granular.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are individualised LBC rates that reflect market sentiment for each of the 118 geographical areas in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, in March 2024, LBC rates were cut 19.2% for non-landed residential use in Tanglin, but increased 14% in the West Coast and Clementi areas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These numbers mirrored the differing market sentiment between suburban and non-suburban sites over the period from September 2023 to March 2024.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, the public knows far less about how land is priced for HDB BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What we do know is that land price for BTO flats takes reference from resale HDB prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It has been stated that the HDB pays fair market value, which is determined by the CV and that the land for public housing is lower compared to private housing in the same area.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, there is no information available to the public about land prices for HDB flats, similar to the chart like the 118 Zone LBC chart, which suggests how the CV adjusts the fair market value of HDB BTO flats in response to rising HDB resale prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is a public demand to better understand and unpack the fair market value determined by the CV for land reserved for HDB.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With well over 80% of all land in Singapore belonging to the state, there is a deep interest in determining the sustainability and affordability of land prices for BTO flats for current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister tell us how the CV discounts the land sold to HDB beyond the general explanation of market principles?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How is this discount derived and what is its basis?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would the Government release zone-specific data on land values for land reserved for BTO flats over time?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In connection with this, how does the Government assure the public and this House that it is not raiding the reserves when it prices land for BTO flats, when the only explanation the public relies on is its reference to the unknown fair market value for HDB land?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Mr Chairman, the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) has benefited many lower-wage Singaporean workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We support this as workers deserve to be paid living wages.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, I have some questions today about the long-term sustainability of the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS) in the context of our overall economy and what MOF's view is, given the Ministry's role in managing Singapore's fiscal policies prudently.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The original WCS co-funding of 40% was supposed to end by 2017, but was instead extended multiple times.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In 2024, instead of decreasing to 15% to 30%, it was raised to 30% to 50%.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am concerned about the ongoing extension of what was presented as temporary support.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In its Budget 2025 wish list, the Singapore National Employers Federation asked that the co-funding of wage increases continue beyond 2026, suggesting a growing dependency on these subsidies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How did our economy get to the point where our businesses rely so on such wage support?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This goes beyond labour policy and I hope for more clarity on how MOF intends to structure an exit plan with firm targets that takes into account a whole-of-economy approach.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A clear exit plan from PWCS has to also take into consideration the overall structure of economy, projections of where we are headed and contain the right ingredients to allow businesses and our overall fiscal structure to remain sustainable in the long run.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will include having a hard look at our overall cost structure beyond labour, including our land policies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With economic disruptions becoming more frequent, will we keep returning to wage subsidies whenever sectors face challenges?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What signals does this send to businesses about long-term planning and productivity investments?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we support wage improvements for workers, we need greater certainty about how these temporary measures fit into Singapore's long-term fiscal and economic policy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Both workers and businesses deserve a clear roadmap for the future beyond the current repeated ad hoc extensions of the supposedly temporary measures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How is MOF enhancing efficiency, fiscal prudence and responsibility in the Budget process?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are not the only ones feeling this pressure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The United States (US) has created a Department of Government Efficiency headed by Mr Elon Musk to treat government inefficiency.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The United Kingdom (UK) Chancellor has announced that the government departments will be asked to identify 5% efficiency savings to crack down on government waste.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To what extent does MOF expect all Ministries and Statutory Boards to improve budget efficiency year-on-year?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can MOF ensure more collaborative initiatives across different Ministries to improve the coordinated delivery of Government services?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How often does the MOF undertake resource reviews and transformation on a whole-of-Government basis in order to sustain a healthy fiscal position?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Chua, you may take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, the reason for my cut on Sovereign Wealth Funds (SWF) transparency is simple.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must demand better standards from the investment managers managing our reserves and take the lead in transparency, accountability and governance standards, as these involve the stewardship of public monies for all Singaporeans, not just its funds' direct shareholders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should aim for transparency in both our public and private market investments, regardless of whether it is held by Government of Singapore Investment Corporation (GIC), Temasek Holdings, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) or even the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board for that matter.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To many market observers, the gold standard, as in most things SWFs-related, is the largest bank investment management – Norway's sovereign wealth fund.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When it comes to transparency, they publicly share a whole suite of details regarding their operations from individual investments, returns before and after fees, even their voting records.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Their chief executive officer (CEO) has a popular podcast, In Good Company, where he interviews portfolio companies and prefaces every interview openly discussing fund ownership details.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: They prove you can be transparent and perform well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On transparency, however, Singapore's sovereign funds are falling short.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do not think they assess the performance of the third-party fund managers they are invested in merely on a five-year basis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand the rationale of not disclosing its assets on the management, but hiding performance figures does not make sense and merely raises questions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I notice that Temasek Holdings is invested in not just private markets, but many of these investment structures are also increasingly complex, perhaps a reflection of the investment landscape today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A Business Times article dated 12 October 2024 was titled, "Temasek CIO Gets Behind Asset-Shuffling Funds Snubbed by Others".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It further goes on to say that the chief investment officer of a Singaporean state-owned investor voiced unusual enthusiasm for continuation funds in which private equity managers shift hard-to-sell assets from an older vehicle into a brand new one.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The repackaged assets are then offered to investors, such as Temasek, known as limited partners.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, these harder-to-value investments need more oversight, not less.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, they are becoming less transparent even as investments get more complex.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In accounting, Level 3 financial assets require significant use of internal models and assumptions to estimate fair value as reliable market data is not readily available.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, listed companies have to disclose in their annual reports details of valuation methodologies and the assumptions made in their financial statements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is a glaring contradiction in all of these, in that even as the Government and Temasek demand good corporate governance from the companies that they invest in, they are secretive about their own performance and remuneration matrix.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, we must demand better standards from the investment managers managing our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Any attempts to deflect this via operational independence must be rejected.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singaporeans compare prices to get the best value for money for their purchases and to better manage the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: According to the 2023 Household Expenditure Survey, about 16% of Singaporeans' monthly expenditure is on food and beverage (F&B) services.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Unfortunately, it is more complicated to compare prices when eating out than when making other retail purchases.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While some F&B outlets display all-inclusive prices, others do not include service charge and Goods and Services Tax (GST) in the menu price.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Their inconsistency can cause frustration when the customer sees the final bill, which is almost 20% higher than the menu price.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It also makes it harder for customers to compare prices across different F&B operators.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Tourism is a key driver of our services industry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have, in the past, often heard feedback from my foreign friends about how they are shocked by the final prices of their F&B purchases and their taxi rides compared to the prices they were initially expecting.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the era of ride hailing apps, the shock of seeing a myriad of additional charges added to the flag-down fare is now much less likely.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But when it comes to F&B establishments, the sticker shock remains.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: IRAS' rationale for this concession was to help restaurants manage operational challenges when waiving service charge for takeaway orders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given the prevalence of electronic menus, it is very straightforward for restaurants to display both dine-in and takeaway prices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, if they use paper menus, they could simply give a 10% discount for takeaway orders instead of having 10% for dine-in orders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Some restaurants do display all-inclusive prices, but many may be reluctant to do so for fear that they will be seen as more expensive than their competitors.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, users may face difficulties when redeeming their CDC Vouchers due to its fixed denomination and expiry dates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The list of participating merchants could also be expanded to include food courts within privately owned commercial properties and pharmacies located within HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Discounts for CHAS, Merdeka and Pioneer Generation cardholders have been offered by establishments, such as FairPrice, Unity and store holders within certain hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Under the new scheme, however, these rebates will be borne by the Government instead, in a more equitable manner.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, Government support could also be easily accessed by those experiencing difficulties obtaining CDC Vouchers via the appeal processes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: By expanding the CHAS, Merdeka and Pioneer Generation programme to provide discounts for daily necessities, the cost-of-living pressures faced by Singaporeans could be easily, equitably, elegantly and efficiently paid.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, I would like to declare my interest as CEO of the Wealth Management Institute, which hosts the Asia Centre for Changemakers, Asia's learning lab for impact philanthropy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Philanthropy has always been a part of Singapore's DNA.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore has long provided generous tax incentives of up to 250% for donations to local charities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, to truly cement our position as a leading philanthropy hub, Singapore must broaden its perspective on doing good beyond the traditional definition of donation and grantmaking.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Philanthropy today has the potential to catalyse social innovation and drive systemic solutions to some of the region's most pressing social and environmental challenges.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Reflecting global advancements in the field of philanthropy, impact investing and venture philanthropy have demonstrated their ability to generate meaningful and scalable impact.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Another example is blended finance, which strategically combines concessional and commercial capital to unlock development opportunities that would otherwise remain out of reach.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Through these innovative financing models, philanthropy is emerging as a unique asset class for social progress.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With a higher risk tolerance, longer-term horizon and acceptance of below-market or zero financial returns, it is uniquely positioned to fund nascent social enterprises, de-risk high-impact ventures and bridge funding gaps where commercial capital is hesitant to engage.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By mobilising more capital through a holistic definition of philanthropy, one that includes impact investing, blended finance and catalytic capital, we can accelerate early-stage innovations in uncharted territory.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Notably, this expanded approach has the potential to direct more patient and risk-tolerant capital toward climate initiatives to unlock breakthroughs in renewable energy, carbon capture and sustainable infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our strong financial and regulatory environment, coupled with our reputation as a trusted wealth and asset management hub, provides a solid foundation for mobilising capital effectively.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, to fully realise our ambition of becoming Asia's leading philanthropy hub, we must expand our policy and partnership framework.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, harmonise regulations and incentives for philanthropy and impact capital.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Philanthropy in Singapore currently falls under three separate Ministries' policy domains: the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth, MOF and MAS.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To strengthen our position as a leading philanthropy hub, we need to review and harmonise related laws and policies to ensure greater coherence and effectiveness.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, as we broaden our understanding of philanthropy to include models like impact investing and blended finance, tax incentives should be extended to encourage these approaches while accounting for potential financial returns.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Similarly, while charitable foundations come under the lighter touch grantmakers regime, they still face restrictions from a charity governance framework that inadvertently prevent foundations from engaging in venture philanthropy, as an example, to scale social innovations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Corporations play a critical role in contributing to the communities in which they operate.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Since then, this has catalysed US$6 billion into sectors, such as education, healthcare and social assistance, in India.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: A vibrant philanthropic hub requires a strong public-private-people coalition to shape strategic direction and drive ecosystem alignment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This coalition will provide strategic leadership and momentum to scale Singapore's role as a philanthropy hub.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It could also be tasked with developing a national philanthropy roadmap, including a plan to align philanthropic capital with Asia's green financing commitments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, Singapore's fiscal prudence has long been a pillar of our economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The time taken from ideation to budget allocation and, ultimately, project implementation represents an economic cost by itself.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SMEs and startups often face challenges in assessing Government procurement opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many SMEs and promising startups with innovative solutions struggle to participate in Government procurement due to administrative and track record requirements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can MOF facilitate greater SME and startup participation in Government tenders?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Are there measures in place to ensure that procurement frameworks do not disproportionately disadvantage SMEs and promising startups and the Government missing out on promising solutions?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond procurement, the cost of doing business in Singapore remains a key concern.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Complex regulations and high compliance costs often prevent SMEs from scaling up effectively.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The adage, "Time is money" could not be more apt for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ultimately, improving efficiency benefits both businesses and the economy as Singapore strives to remain competitive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ensuring that Government processes are streamlined, procurement is accessible and businesses can operate with greater agility will be critical.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I look forward to MOF's insights on these issues.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: One positive outcome from the Government Procurement framework, Whole-of-Government Period Contract and Framework Agreement (WOG PCFA) for creative services and for video and animation services, is that public sector agencies are more aware of SME creative agencies and their services.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The UK's Public Services (Social Value) Act 2012 requires public authorities and their supply chains to go beyond cost consideration to also consider how the public authority can make a positive economic, social and/or environmental impact through the procurement process.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: At the debate on the Motion on supporting families this February, I had suggested for the Government to consider embedding social value into Government procurement framework.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Under such an arrangement, public sector agencies would have the discretion to determine their social value commitments alongside the core contract deliverables.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, under the WOG PCFAs and standard procurement for creative services as well as video and animation services, public sector agencies that procure creative services or video and animation services could specify hiring, upscaling and training of the local workforce as a social value objective in the contract delivery.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This would give impetus to creative agencies working on Government projects to engage Singaporean creative freelancers, rather than to prioritise cost and thus outsource to overseas market.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Embedding local workforce upscaling as a social value objective ensures that Singaporean creative freelancers have a safe space to unlearn and relearn new skills and technology.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This matters because many Singaporean creative freelancers are battling unprecedented levels of offshoring and substitution of creative labour with generative AI.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In response to fellow Member Usha Chandradas' Parliamentary Question (PQ) on the growth prospects of the creative economy, the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth replied, "There are many opportunities for creative practitioners, especially if they are able to capitalise on growing demands and trends, such as leveraging technology and working with regional and international partners to reach audiences beyond Singapore.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, the social value outcomes for the public sector agencies could be supporting Singaporean creative freelancers to build expertise and track record to pitch for higher value creative work in and outside of Singapore." Likewise, Government schools could uplift the prospects and capabilities of Singaporean freelance coaches and instructors delivering co-curricular activities (CCA) to students, if schools, too, embedded similar social value objective of hiring, upscaling and training local workforce in the procurement of CCA instruction.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure that enhancement of social values balanced against other priorities, such as achieving value for money and delivering the core contract deliverables, MOF could guide public sector agencies to engage with potential suppliers on how best to embed social value objectives into the contract delivery, including the tangible and measurable conditions of the contract to be monitored throughout contract delivery.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Embedding social value in Government procurement can be a game changer to strengthen the employability of Singaporean freelancers who are less resource endowed.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang): Singapore's next bound of economic growth can come from strengthening our position as a global hub for startups and innovation.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Government Ministries and agencies can support this by employing the services and products of startups and also benefit from their innovations.

speaker: The Chairman
text: However, startups face a lot of challenges in securing Government business.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Beyond hackathons, pilots and proof of concepts, the reasons are quite understandable.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Startups need more hand-holding, because they are smaller and have less management depth.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There is also always a question of the longevity of a startup as a supplier.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Government procurement is often stacked against younger firms, such as by asking for long track records, or in new innovation areas, procurement officers or buying departments may not yet know enough to define the procurement parameters intelligently.

speaker: The Chairman
text: This feels "lose-lose" for the startups and the Government.

speaker: The Chairman
text: How can we prepare startups to serve Government clients?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, participating in Government tenders present both opportunities and challenges for our SMEs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Projects involving emerging and advanced technology innovations are valuable opportunities for startups and smaller businesses with innovative solutions to participate in.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, these companies often face challenges in meeting the financial requirements for Government tenders and providing a proven track record.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For such projects, will MOF consider measures to enable these companies to participate and in support of innovation?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Cash flow is critical to SMEs in managing their operational expenses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Suppliers for Government contracts are able to submit invoices electronically to track and receive notifications on payment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Has this helped to ensure timely payment to suppliers?

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their questions and suggestions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will cover how MOF agencies are simplifying rules for businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Shawn Huang will address improving the experience of transacting with the Government and making government procurement more accessible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, ensuring responsible, effective and efficient use of our public resources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Third, preparing for Singapore to meet intensifying, long-term challenges, particularly climate change and strengthening our social compact for a more caring and inclusive society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked what MOF agencies are doing to simplify rules for a more pro-business environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Rules and regulations exist for several reasons, from safeguarding people, property and the environment, to ensuring good governance and accountability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government has to strike a balance between these important objectives and the need to encourage enterprise and innovation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Therefore, Singapore's approach has been to enact practical rules and review them regularly to streamline and remove outdated ones.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Currently, businesses expecting to cross the one million taxable turnover threshold within the next 12 months must register for and start charging GST within a month of forecast.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This timeline can be tight for some SMEs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, IRAS will progressively expand the requirement for intermediaries to pre-fill income information on behalf of self-employed persons (SEPs).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: About 87% of individual taxpayers today benefit from pre-filled income information by their employers and intermediaries for their income tax filing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, many SEPs do not enjoy this convenience.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The intermediaries that engage the services of SEPs already have the income information of the SEPs and are in a good position to provide this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is more efficient for them to do so than to have the individual SEPs fill in the information in their respective tax returns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We started by requiring commission-paying intermediaries, such as real estate agencies and insurance providers, to submit income information for their agents and this has benefited over 100,000 self-employed commission agents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: IRAS plans to bring more intermediaries on board.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It has been encouraging and engaging private hire car and taxi operators, as well as the delivery platforms, and I urge these intermediaries to come on board as soon as possible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have also been simplifying rules where we can.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One example is the Fixed Expense Deduction Ratio (FEDR), which allows qualifying businesses the option of claiming their tax deductions for business expenses based on a prescribed percentage of their gross income earned.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is simpler and more convenient, compared to using actual allowable business expenses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The FEDR was first introduced in year of assessment 2019 for private hire car and taxi drivers and subsequently extended to commission agents and delivery workers, and the utilisation has been high, which shows that this is a good option for many of our workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will be consulting stakeholders on how the FEDR can be expanded to support more small businesses and self-employed persons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are reducing and removing regulations where possible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: IRAS will drop the requirement for second-hand goods' dealers to seek approval before using the GST gross margin scheme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The scheme allows second-hand goods' dealers to charge GST on the gross margin of the sale, rather than the full sale price.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is because GST is often priced into the base cost from earlier transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As most dealers are generally compliant with the scheme's requirements, IRAS will remove the need for them to obtain approval starting from 1 July this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will streamline the compliance process, particularly for new or smaller second-hand goods dealers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is a requirement today for companies to disclose their directors' interest in shares or debentures in the director's statement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the years, ACRA has received an increasing number of requests from companies to be exempted from this requirement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In cases where all the company shareholders agree, ACRA will grant these exemption requests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Information of the company's shareholding will remain publicly accessible and this maintains corporate transparency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These are part of the ongoing efforts to improve our rules and processes and, in the interest of time, I am not able to share the full range, but this is an ongoing work and we will continue to engage businesses and also our frontline officers, our colleagues, solicit their ideas to jointly improve our regulatory landscape.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This approach is also in line with the spirit of Forward Singapore (Forward SG).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It reinforces in our agencies the importance of working with citizens and businesses while taking on board their feedback to continually improve our policies, rules and processes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are continually looking at how we can transform and improve the way we operate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about resource reviews and improving budget efficiency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our budgeting framework is designed with efficiency in mind.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We regularly review the block budgets for Ministries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOF also applies controls to spending and manpower growth to drive agency transformation and yield savings, which are then returned to MOF for central reallocation towards emerging priorities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Mr Saktiandi that it is important to have strong collaboration and coordination across Ministries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOF actively encourages coordinated service delivery where there are synergies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They offer residents one-stop access to about 600 government services from over 25 agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Resourcing levers can be used to drive transformation on a whole-of-Government basis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This provides agencies seed funding to pilot innovative and transformative ideas if the proposals involve interagency collaboration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to deliver our projects in an efficient and cost-effective manner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We regularly review our internal processes to improve efficiencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For instance, we shortened the Gateway evaluation for large development projects to speed up the approval process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Liang highlighted the need to continually enhance effectiveness and governance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is supported by programme evaluation, which helps us to understand whether a programme is achieving its objectives and whether improvements are needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But as Prime Minister always reminds us, it does not mean that today, we are perfect.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is still room for improvement and we will work hard to make those continuous improvements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is something that we will continue to do.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Louis Chua asked about the concession for hotel and F&B establishments that impose a service charge to display GST-exclusive prices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This concession was granted in 1994, based on industry feedback that it would be costly and operationally challenging to maintain and display separate price lists for take-away items and dine-in items, as service charge would be imposed only on the latter.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The concession is to help reduce business costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But clarity for consumers is also important, and businesses that rely on this concession must display a prominent statement informing consumers that prices shown are subject to service charge and GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This practice has now been in place for three decades, and we last reviewed it again in 2022.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Conversely, removing the concession may lead to more confusion and also increase costs for businesses as they would now need to print multiple sets of menus and price lists.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will review closer to the date whether to continue or to stop bearing in mind the economic conditions at that time because we are in a more uncertain global environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The PWCS is not a broad-based subsidy for all companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To get PWCS, the employer has to pay their low-wage workers a wage increase.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Then, they can qualify to get this co-funding from the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, the purpose is for the Government to co-fund and to share some of the costs of helping our lower-wage workers to earn a higher income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Because we want employers to pay their lower-wage workers a higher salary, we share with the employers part of this cost of paying the lower-wage workers a higher salary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And this is an important part of our social compact, which I think Ms He will agree with.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I do not think Ms He is suggesting that we should stop providing support for employers, especially our SMEs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am quite confident she is not saying that.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If I look at the other schemes that we have in place to improve productivity, which I also agree with Ms He is an important priority.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, this is not in lieu of those other schemes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In fact, this is something that we put in place specifically to help employers to be able to share some of the costs where they are paying their lower-wage workers a higher salary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But on productivity, we have many other schemes that we will continue to work through our trade associations and chambers, our industry associations with our companies, as well as with our Labour Movement, through the Company Training Committees, to be able to help companies to improve productivity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Because I agree with Ms He that for the wage increases to be sustainable, it must go together with productivity improvements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I just make an observation here that what Ms He is saying seems to be a little bit different from what Assoc Prof Jamus Lim said during the Budget debate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If I heard him correctly, he suggested that wage increases can happen with or without productivity improvements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But I do agree with Ms He's point that the two, over time, need to move in tandem.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Liang spoke about responsible management of our fiscal resources and reserves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Saktiandi asked how the Government ensures fiscal prudence and responsibility.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have spent within our means and planned ahead for structural spending needs, like rising healthcare expenditure and climate adaptation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This allows the Government to follow through on our commitments, without borrowing or using more of our reserves for immediate needs and recurrent spending.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This fiscal discipline of maintaining a balanced Budget has worked well for Singapore and we must strive to sustain this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our reserves, which have been carefully managed over generations, are another source of strength and national resilience, especially during a crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: During the Global Financial Crisis and COVID-19 pandemic, our reserves protected Singaporeans and placed us in a better position than many other countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We were able to use our reserves for public health, social and economic support measures that saved lives and livelihoods, and enabled Singapore to bounce back and emerge stronger.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our Past Reserves also generate a sustainable and steady stream of income that goes into our Budget every year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Louis Chua spoke about the importance of transparency, accountability and governance of our investment entities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are structures and processes in place to ensure that our investment entities, GIC and Temasek, are good stewards of our reserves for the benefit of all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On governance, the Government ensures that each entity has a competent Board in place to oversee its Management.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government holds the Board accountable for instilling good corporate governance and achieving good long-term returns according to its mandate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At the same time, the Government does not direct or influence the investment decisions of our investment entities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This segregation of roles allows our investment entities to invest professionally with a long-term orientation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And that is why during the Prime Minister's Office's COS earlier on MAS, Mr Chua also acknowledged that it would not be a good idea for the Government to require GIC to invest part of its portfolio in the local equities market.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On transparency, we have put out a lot of information on our reserves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Temasek's net portfolio value and MAS' official foreign reserves are public information.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: All our entities publish information on their portfolio returns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On performance, the Government does not look at one single parameter.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Neither do we focus only on short-term performance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our investment entities have performed creditably over the long term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Given the increase in market volatility in recent years, some variation from market indices is to be expected, and what is key is that our entities continue to navigate the uncertainty while maintaining a disciplined long-term approach to generating sustainable returns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Stewardship and accountability are key principles that we abide by in managing the reserves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have benefited from the careful work of previous generations, and this Government believes that we must continue to maintain the same fiscal discipline and provide a strong financial foundation for both current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Before I do my reply, I just wish to seek a clarification from Mr Louis Chua so that I can respond to his cut properly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In his cut, as I understand it, he mentioned CDC Vouchers being applicable to all.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, I just was not sure of what Mr Chua's position was.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Indeed, I also mentioned in the Budget speech I gave earlier that that was the evolution of the CDC Voucher Scheme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Or is Mr Chua saying, keep CDC Vouchers in its present form and then, in addition, have this new scheme.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I think that that is an option which that the Ministry can consider.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: But the whole idea is that this is another option in which we can go back to that sort of system, whereby the so-called CDC Vouchers are given to those who are in the lower-, middle-income households.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, I am not sure that exactly answered my question but that is alright.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will deal with it when I come to the reply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked what MOF agencies are doing to help prepare Singapore for climate change and environmental sustainability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is not a light undertaking and requires a whole-of-nation effort.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have developed new fiscal tools, like green bonds under the Significant Infrastructure Government Loan Act, to catalyse our green financing market and support our longer-term spending needs for environmental sustainability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MOF has also established the Singapore Green Bond Framework, the second edition of which was released last month.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are also incorporating sustainability considerations into government procurement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We aim to extend this to all government procurement by 2028, in a manner that keeps pace with industry readiness and international developments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Participating in green government procurement is an opportunity for our businesses to build the track record to meet demands of buyers, investors and consumers who are seeking greener goods and services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government will be introducing mandatory climate-related disclosures in a phased approach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To help companies ease into the new reporting requirements, they can tap the Sustainability Reporting Grant and the SME Sustainability Reporting Programme to kickstart their journey.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: ACRA is also taking steps to grow sustainability reporting and assurance capabilities in Singapore, and build a robust pipeline of professionals in this area.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will also create more good job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Louis Chua spoke about the need for a strong social compact.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Indeed, Forward SG was an exercise in refreshing our social compact.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The insights gained from the exercise have found their way into many of the measures in the Budget.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In his Budget speech, Prime Minister spoke about how the Government is fostering a more caring and inclusive society, one where every Singaporean feels valued and supported.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Inclusivity cannot be created through government policy interventions alone.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It needs the collective effort of all of society.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will spur collective efforts in three ways.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, we will continue to encourage individuals and businesses to give back to society.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We offer 250% tax deductions on qualifying donations made by individuals and corporates.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under the Corporate Volunteer Scheme, corporates can also receive 250% tax deductions on wages and qualifying expenses when employees volunteer, provide services, or are seconded to Institutions of Public Character.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Foo suggested going further to encourage corporate giving, taking inspiration from India's 2% mandatory corporate social responsibility spending law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We agree with the intent of Ms Foo's suggestion, which is to encourage corporates to contribute.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, we are doing so in a different way.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Through tax incentives, we encourage and support corporate philanthropy and allow businesses to contribute based on their own corporate values and business models.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Requiring profitable companies to contribute a certain percentage of profits to corporate social responsibility would take the decision and initiative out of the hands of corporates and be contrary to the spirit of philanthropy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also provide donation-matching grant schemes, such as Tote Board's Enhanced Fund-Raising Programme (EFR), to amplify the impact of donations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: During the pandemic, we raised matching support under the EFR from 20% to 100% to galvanise community giving.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As the Prime Minister announced at Budget 2025, the Government and Tote Board will provide an extension of dollar-for-dollar matching for FY2025 in support of SG60.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This enhanced support will gradually taper, reverting to pre-COVID-19 levels in FY2027.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Through the EFR, SG Gives and other initiatives, the Government and Tote Board will set aside more than $600 million in matching funds to strengthen our spirit of giving.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As we celebrate SG60, I hope Singaporeans will reflect on how far we have come together and donate generously.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, the Tote Board will allocate resources to support collaborations amongst Singaporeans who use their time and talent to uplift the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Tote Board's Enabling Lives Initiative (ELI) Grant supports community partnerships that benefit persons with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Recently, a team of researchers, engineers, physiotherapists and social workers used the ELI grant to develop a device that translates minute finger movements into software controls.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It enables persons with muscular dystrophy to use smart devices even in advanced stages of their condition.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The product has tested well and the team is planning to scale up its deployment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Third, we are strengthening impact measurement capabilities across the non-profit ecosystem to maximise the social impact of our grants.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These efforts will allow Tote Board, as a grant-maker, to optimise resource allocation and spur the social sector towards greater effectiveness.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I come now to Mr Louis Chua's cut.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It still was not quite clear to me whether he was saying to do away with the CDC Vouchers or not.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the original gist of the cut, he suggested that it should only be limited to the lower-income, but when I sought clarification, it was not quite clear.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will just take it at face value.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, many Singaporeans remain anxious about cost-of-living pressures.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such concerns and anxieties are not limited to lower-income households.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Recognising this, the Government intentionally designed the CDC Vouchers Scheme as a broad-based measure to provide support and assurance for all Singaporean households.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It initially started out as a small scheme for the lower-income, but recognising these cost pressures on all households, something which has been echoed in this Chamber by many Workers' Party speakers, the Government extended it to all households.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is not to say, however, that we do not have other schemes which are targeted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I note Mr Chua called to redesign a scheme, although it is not clear whether this is in addition to CDC Vouchers or not, to provide more targeted support for daily necessities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He referenced the Blue and Orange CHAS cards as a way of triaging or indicating who would be eligible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I see that Mr Chua has drawn inspiration from the CHAS Blue and Orange cardholders' scheme that NTUC FairPrice has launched and which takes effect, I think, in the first quarter of 2025.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) is doing that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the fact of the matter is that the Government already has in place a comprehensive system of targeted support in which the lower-income receives much more.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under the enhanced Assurance Package and the permanent GST Voucher Scheme, households with less means can get more cash transfers as well as larger rebates for utilities, and service and conservancy charges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On top of these, the Prime Minister increased the rates for ComCare assistance schemes in this Budget to better support lower-income and vulnerable families with basic living expenses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also recently enhanced Workfare and Silver Support to provide targeted structural support to vulnerable groups.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include lower-wage workers and seniors with low incomes in their working years who now have less savings in retirement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If one looks at the system of government subsidies and transfers as a whole, you will see that the Government has put in place a progressive system that provides more for those with less.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Prime Minister just showed earlier a chart in his round-up speech a couple of hours ago where, in short, everyone benefits from government spending, but the lower-income and the vulnerable receive more.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will now turn to the Leader of the Opposition Pritam Singh's cut.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Singh wanted to know why there is no information available to the public about land prices for HDB flats, similar to the 118-zone Land Betterment Charge (LBC) Table of Rates, and how the Chief Valuer (CV) assesses the value of land purchased by HDB to build flats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, there are two parts to his cut: first, the comparison to the LBC Table of Rates; and second, how the CV assesses the value of the land.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the comparison to the LBC Table of Rates (LBC TOR) is misconceived.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The general principle is that rates or valuations are made known to parties who would have to pay the fee or price.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The LBC is a tax payable on the enhancement in land value arising from modifications landowners make to their land.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Any landowner can make this request to modify their land, such as to intensify the use of the land, and this is subject to approval by the Urban Redevelopment Authority or Singapore Land Authority.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Following this approval, they would have to pay the LBC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are several hundred LBC transactions in any given year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For ease of tax administration, we have a Table of Rates (TOR) instead of valuing each transaction individually.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This TOR is made public so that the parties who need to make payment know how much they have to pay.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, the CV could also do a site-specific, or what we call a spot, valuation of the land value enhancement for each case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This happens if the landowner opts for it for precision or if the LBC TOR is not applicable, such as when the current or proposed new use do not fall within a comparable use group within the LBC TOR.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For this spot valuation, the CV would use established valuation methodologies consistent with how she values any state land for sale.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this instance, the spot valuation outcome is made known to the requesting party as the potential paying party but not to the general public at large.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The valuation outcome is made known to HDB as the paying party.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not necessary to put out a public table of rates like the LBC TOR as there are no other buyers for these sites.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In all three instances, whether it is the LBC TOR, the spot valuations for landowners or HDB, the CV uses established valuation methodologies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Singh asked how the CV discounts the land sold to the HDB.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: HDB pays fair market value for state land.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The fair market value is determined by the CV using established valuation principles.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This approach would be no different from that of other professional valuers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The normal approach is to reference comparable transactions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Private housing transactions would not be a suitable reference as public housing has restrictions, such as more stringent eligibility criteria.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is the fair market value of land intended for the purposes of public housing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: By putting the fair market value of land into the reserves, we preserve the value of our reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The financial proceeds of the sale are invested to grow them for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Fifty percent of the investment returns on our reserves supplement the annual Budget through the NIRC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This careful approach of managing our reserves strikes a balance between the needs of current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Singh also made a reference to BTO flats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He said, "What we do know is that the land price for BTO flats take reference from resale HDB prices.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With the increase in resale flat prices for 2024, there is inevitably a serious concern about whether land for HDB BTO flats is priced sustainably or if growing subsidies are going to be needed in the future." So, that is the question of the price of the BTO unit, not the price of the land that HDB purchased.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have actually answered this many times before, but let me just do a very quick summary.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The issue of land costs should not be conflated with BTO affordability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The land cost is the amount paid by HDB for the land.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is different from the flat price, which is what the BTO flat buyer pays HDB for the unit.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: BTO flat pricing is based on affordability, not cost.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And we have explained this many times before.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: HDB first establishes the market value of the flats by considering the prevailing market conditions, the prices of comparable resale flats nearby and the individual attributes of the flats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It then applies a subsidy to ensure that BTO flats are affordable for Singaporeans across different income levels.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The pricing of BTO flats is therefore not based on the land cost of the flats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do not pass land cost through to the BTO buyer.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have one of the highest home ownership rates in the world, with 90% of households owning their own homes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our BTO system plays an integral part in keeping public housing affordable for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This means they were able to service their monthly mortgage repayments with their monthly CPF contributions, with little to no cash outlay.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This has remained stable in the past few years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have also taken steps to ensure that BTO flats remain affordable and accessible to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: HDB will provide additional subsidies to those buying Plus and Prime flats on top of the significant market discounts that already apply to all BTO flats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And to ensure fairness, we impose tighter restrictions and a subsidy recovery rate commensurate with the extent of additional subsidies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Over the past five years, we have ramped up our BTO supply significantly to meet Singaporeans' demand for housing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our approach ensures that BTO flats remain affordable and accessible to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to keep it that way.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Mr Chairman, I will address Members' questions and suggestions on government procurement and how we can improve the experience of transacting with the Government.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Our procurement rules are designed to uphold open and fair competition, achieve value for money and manage project risks.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: But we need to take care that these do not result in heavy compliance costs for our businesses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Improving access to government procurement is a win-win for Government and businesses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The Government benefits from the competition fostered by a wider supplier pool, while more businesses can leverage government contracts to build track records.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Ms Jean See asked the Government to consider using Government procurement to strengthen the employability of our freelance creatives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We understand the challenges of keeping up with technological trends and evolving demands, in particular, for freelancers who do not benefit from training typically provided by employers to employees.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: When assessing value for money in procurement, the Government looks for optimal balance between benefits and costs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Benefits can include the achievement of economic, social and environmental objectives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We do take into consideration important social objectives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For example, we require our suppliers to comply with the Progressive Wage Model, where applicable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: However, government procurement requirements must also be non-discriminatory and fair to all businesses, in line with our international trade obligations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Ms Jean See's objectives to strengthen the employability of freelancers is important and it can be addressed through resources and programmes the Government has put in place.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: These include the substantial support that we provide to all Singaporeans for their training needs, such as the SkillsFuture Career Transition Programme and SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, which the Prime Minister covered in his Budget Speech.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Workforce Singapore (WSG) and SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) also provide a range of resources to help individuals with their training decisions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For example, SkillsFuture Jobs-Skills Insights publications are useful references for individuals, including freelancers, seeking to reskill or upskill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Creatives in the arts sector can also look to the National Arts Council's (NAC's) Capability Development Grant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This grant can support up to 90% of the training activity or programme costs for SEPs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: NAC's Art Resource Hub also provides resources, spaces and networking opportunities for SEPs in the arts sector.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: These include mentorships and career guidance to help SEPs in their professional career development as well as resources that can help SEPs with relevant business and legal knowledge.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: In support of entrepreneurial efforts, we will continue to make government procurement opportunities more accessible to our businesses, including small businesses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This year, MOF will introduce two additional initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: First, we will expand Tender Lite, an initiative first rolled out in April 2024 to streamline procurement conditions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Second, we will make it easier for businesses participating in tenders that require innovative solutions, to progress from pilot to deployment at scale.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We will introduce a new initiative, Innovative Procurement Partnership.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Edward Chia talked about making it easier for smaller businesses to access government procurement opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Ms Tan asked for an update on Tender Lite's effectiveness and whether the Government would consider expanding Tender Lite to other sectors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: About 90% of businesses who responded to our survey provided feedback that the simpler conditions of contract in Tender Lite made participation in government tenders easier.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: MOF has been working closely with industry stakeholders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: These include the Singapore Business Federation (SBF), the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises (ASME) and sector-specific Trade Associations to further develop Tender Lite.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We will be expanding Tender Lite to construction and information and communications technology (ICT) contracts, which will benefit businesses in these sectors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We will be simplifying the conditions for closing of accounts or conclusion of projects.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We will cap the liquidated damages at 10% of contract value and remove the need for security deposits.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We will also remove or shorten the Defects Liability Period where possible.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: These changes will help to ease contractors' cashflow.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Tender Lite for ICT contracts will be implemented in phases from the second half of this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Consultations with industry are ongoing and details will be published in due course.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Next, let me touch on the new Innovative Procurement Partnership.
